The History of the Dichotomy of Civic Western and Ethnic Eastern 
Nationalism 
The dichotomy of civic vs. ethnic nationalism has long been applied spatially to explain 
differences between ‘Western’ and ‘Eastern’ manifestations of nationalism. Though 
frequently criticised on empirical, methodological, and normative grounds, this dualism 
continues to find widespread use in nationalism studies. Through a genealogical study 
of the dichotomy’s emergence and evolution from Hans Kohn to John Plamenatz and 
Ernest Gellner, the article traces its strong ties to discourses and policies of ‘Western’ 
superiority, and to demi-orientalising constructions of ‘Eastern Europe’ as the inferior 
other of the ‘civilized West’. 
Keywords: Western and Eastern nationalism; the civic-ethnic dichotomy; Hans Kohn; 
John Plamenatz; Ernest Gellner 
 
Introduction 
In a 2009 essay, Brian Porter-Szűcs, a prominent scholar of Polish history, lamented that 
Hans Kohn’s dichotomy of a good nationalism in ‘the West’ and a bad nationalism in ‘the 
East’ remained influential. ‘Though repeatedly debunked, the spatial embodiment of 
nationalism’s Janus face continues to resurface’, Porter-Szűcs argued, using John Plamenatz 
(1973), Rogers Brubaker (1992) and Liah Greenfeld (1992) as his main examples (2009, p. 
5). Critique of the civic/Western – ethnic/Eastern dichotomy has not abated since 2009, but 
nor has its continued application. The dichotomy frequently appears in contemporary 
scholarship, for example in works by political scientists using it in multiple country 
quantitative data analysis (Coakley, 2018; Larsen, 2017; Schulman, 2002). 
 
Like other research fields in the humanities and social sciences, nationalism studies 
have frequently turned to dualistic oppositions as analytical tools. In 1998, Philip Spencer 
and Howard Wollman compiled a ‘cursory list’ of no less than twenty dualistic distinctions 
common in the literature of nationalism. Although not all have been normatively charged or 
applied spatially, the authors observed that ‘[t]he contrasts specifically between West and 
East, between the political and the cultural, between the civic and ethnic, between the liberal 
and illiberal are all … hewn from the same rock’ (Spencer and Wollman, 1998, p. 257). This 
observation forms the starting point of the following argument. Some scholars have used a 
civic-ethnic nationalism dichotomy for analytical purposes without linking it to a macro-

--- PAGE 3 ---
2 
 
spatial West-East opposition, but historically and in its most prominent articulations, the civic 
vs. ethnic nationalism dichotomy has remained inherently linked to an opposition of West 
and East. This linking is the topic of this paper. 
 
By tracing its genealogy, I will seek to show that this dichotomy of civic/Western – 
ethnic/Eastern nationalism has been firmly embedded in broader, orientalising discourses that 
define ‘Eastern Europe’/‘the East’ as the inferior Other of ‘Western Europe’/‘the West.’ In 
constructing the Eastern Other in this way, these discourses have simultaneously constructed 
Western Europe/the West as a normative authority, epistemologically equipped with a 
sanitised self-image of civic, liberal virtue. Epistemological ordering, I argue, prepares the 
ground for political ordering; it legitimizes the perpetuation of the political subject position of 
Western Europe/the West. This may help to explain why this dichotomy – despite decades of 
critique and deconstruction – remains influential in scholarship and beyond. But before we 
embark on the genealogical study, we must examine some recent critiques of the dichotomy 
in order to clarify the main issues at stake. 
 
Contemporary critiques of the Kohn dichotomy 
The 2016 Wiley Blackwell Encyclopedia of Race, Ethnicity, and Nationalism contains an 
entry on Civic and Ethnic Nationalism, written by Aviel Roshwald. For Roshwald (2016, p. 
402): 
“civic nationalism” denotes the claims of legitimacy for, and the sense of commitment 
to, the exercise of territorial sovereignty by (or in the name of) a people with a shared 
political identity. The common rights, duties, and values of citizenship, irrespective of 
any ethnic or cultural differences among the citizenry, are considered to constitute the 
foundation of peoplehood in this framework; in theory, statehood is the forge of 
nationhood.  
‘Ethnic nationalism,’ by contrast, ‘derives its force from a sense of kinship and a myth of 
shared ancestry that is thought to predate statehood’ (ibid). Civic nationalism, the author 
continues, has often been associated with states in Western Europe and the USA and the latter 
with other regions of the world, adding that ‘the contrasting typologies have been linked to 
starkly drawn normative and geocultural differences’ (ibid.). After outlining the history of the 
typology and presenting some critiques of the civic-ethnic dichotomy (Brubaker, 2004; 
Kymlicka, 1995; Kuzio, 2002, etc.), Roshwald concludes (2016, p. 405):

Regional Income Dispersion and Market Potential in the Late 
Nineteenth Century Habsburg Empire∗
Max-Stephan Schulze 
 
 
Abstract 
This paper presents new regional GDP estimates for the Habsburg Monarchy and 
constructs measures of market potential for its 22 major regions. The paper argues 
that regional income differentials were significantly larger, that intra-empire 
catching-up of poor with rich regions was far more limited and that the empire’s 
Eastern regions were much further behind Western Europe than suggested in the 
historiography. The measurement of regional market potential proves strongly 
sensitive to the composition of foreign economies considered in the computations 
and the choice of regional ‘nodes’. Further, though being ‘remote’ imposed some 
penalty, there was no uniform relationship between changes in regions’ relative 
GDP position and their market potential. 
 
 
1. 
Introduction 
The profound regional differences in geography, resource 
endowments and income across Austria-Hungary and issues of regional 
division of labour are recurrent themes in the Habsburg historiography 
(Good 1984; Gross 1973; Freudenberger, 2003; Komlos 1983). In the 
1990s, David Good made a persistent effort to quantify regional product in 
the Habsburg domains as a means to assess the economic lag of East-
Central Europe (Good 1991, 1994, 1997; Good and Ma 1998). According to 
the 1998 estimates, the poorest region in Austria-Hungary enjoyed per 
capita incomes that on the eve of the First World War, and after a long 
process of industrialization in the western regions stretching back to the late

Patterns of growth and stagnation in the
late nineteenth century Habsburg
economy
MAX-STEPHAN SCHULZE
Department of Economic History, London School of Economics, Houghton
Street, London WCA AE
This article addresses two issues that feature prominently in the recent
historiography. First, how does the Habsburg Empire’s economic
performance compare to the record for other European economies in
terms of levels and growth of national income? Second, to what extent
was the Austrian economy subject to prolonged stagnation after ?
These questions are examined on the basis of new annual estimates of
GDP for Austria and Hungary for  to . The article argues, first,
that over the whole period under review Austrian per capita income failed
to expand at a pace broadly commensurate with the country’s relative
income position. The Austrian economy did not catch up with the 
leaders and failed to keep pace with other ‘followers’. Second, the
Hungarian economy recorded a markedly higher rate of per capita income
growth, placing it about mid-range in a European growth comparison.
Third, the new evidence supports the notion of a ‘great depression’ in the
western half of the empire (Austria) after . The distinct periodicity
and differential rates of Austrian and Hungarian growth are consistent
with the argument that the outflow of Austrian capital to Hungary after
the  Vienna stock market crash was crucial in prolonging economic
stagnation in Austria, whilst fuelling the first widespread wave of
industrialisation in Hungary. The reversal of this capital outflow in the
early s was associated with an increase in Austrian economic growth
and a decrease in Hungary’s rate of expansion.
. Introduction
The Habsburg Empire, one of the largest economies on the European
Continent before , rarely features in comparative studies of long-run
growth for, it seems, two major reasons. First, the empire was dissolved in
the aftermath of the First World War and gave way to a multitude of suc-
cessor states. Consequently, the Habsburg economy cannot be included
readily in comparative data sets that encompass the twentieth century.
Second, much of Central and Eastern Europe lies in a ‘statistical dark age’
compared to Western Europe (Good ).

--- PAGE 3 ---
This article presents new annual estimates of GDP for Austria and
Hungary for  to . These estimates are used to address two issues
that feature prominently in the recent historiography. First, how does the
Habsburg Empire’s economic performance compare to the record for other
European economies in terms of levels and growth of national income?
Williamson () argued recently that the late nineteenth century wit-
nessed a process of rapid growth and convergence in living standards, at
least among those countries that now form the OECD. Poor countries at
the European periphery tended to grow faster than the developed
economies at the centre and often even faster than the richer countries over-
seas in the New World, while most of the Third World and Eastern Europe
did not share in this experience. Placed somewhere midrange on the west-
east developmental gradient in Europe and displaying a similar pattern of
regional disparities within its own boundaries (Good ), where does the
Habsburg Empire fit in? Second, to what extent did the Austrian economy
experience prolonged stagnation after  (Komlos , März ,
Schulze )?
The first attempt at a systematic estimation of national income in the
Habsburg Empire and its two major subunits, imperial Austria
(Cisleithania) and imperial Hungary (Transleithania), was made during the
First World War (Fellner , Gürtler ). Subsequently, the dissolution
of the empire stimulated Fellner () and Waizner () to determine
pre-war income levels in the successor-state units. These calculations were
concerned solely with income levels in – and no attempt was made to
derive estimates for the nineteenth century. This early body of work was
taken up again by Eckstein () who estimated national income and cap-
ital formation in – for Hungary in its interwar boundaries to which
the country reverted after World War II. In the s, Nachum Gross in his
doctoral thesis on Austria’s industrialisation () re-worked Fellner’s
() and Waizner’s () material and complemented it by estimates for
earlier benchmark years. This marked the shift in emphasis from predomi-
nantly qualitative and descriptive work to quantitative-analytical research in
Habsburg economic history.
Much of the initial work in the new vein reflected the search for a major
Rostovian or Gerschenkronian economic discontinuity and has led to new
annual estimates of sectoral production. The most significant quantitative
contributions are the industrial and agricultural production indices of
Komlos (), which are on both methodological and empirical grounds
generally recognised as the best produced so far, and the detailed account
of Austrian agricultural production by Sandgruber (). Rudolph’s
() earlier calculations of industrial output are important in this context
primarily because they form an integral part of the one annual estimate of
Austrian national income that has been produced so far (Kausel ). Its
derivative, which refers to the territories of modern-day Austria, is included

--- PAGE 1 ---
Thirty-Second Annual Robert A. Kann Memorial Lecture
“Where our commonality is necessary…”:
Rethinking the End of the Habsburg Monarchy
PIETER M. JUDSON
A
S THE HUNDREDTH ANNIVERSARY OF NOVEMBER 1918 approaches, this article suggests
some ways in which historians might rethink dominant narratives about the character
of the Habsburg monarchy in its ﬁnal years, the reasons for its collapse, and its complex
legacies to the postwar world. Currently, most accounts that narrate the fall of the empire are
still shaped to some extent by outcomes whose character was deﬁned at the time by the
nationalist architects of the states that replaced the monarchy. Even accounting for a sensible
revisionism of their versions of events over the past century, their general reasoning, their
ideological claims, and their worldviews frame the predominant explanations for why the
monarchy fell when it did. Concomitantly, they continue to inﬂuence our understanding of
the character of the regimes that replaced the monarchy after its fall.
To illustrate the problems historians of both Europe and the Habsburg monarchy face when
it comes to explaining the last half century of the empire’s existence, let me start by reﬂecting on
the way we relate this history to an event that shocked one of Europe’s combatant empires in
1916. This particular event brought tangled issues of nationalism and empire glaringly to the
fore, at a time when the empire in question could ill afford it. On the 24 of April 1916 an
armed nationalist uprising broke out in a peripheral crownland capital of one of Europe’s
empires. The salience of nationalist activism to this incident should make it of special
concern to historians who study the character of Central Europe’s empires. It constituted the
biggest nationalist revolt to occur during the war, and as such, it raised stunning questions
about the loyalty of large parts of both the military and civilian populations to the empire.
The rebel nationalists used their violent insurrection to try to establish political autonomy for
their ethnic nation. Yet the revolt did not gain the level of mass support its leaders had expected
from ordinary citizens across the crownland, many of whom may have been relatively
indifferent to the nationalist cause, given the quotidian challenges of wartime survival they
faced on the home front. Nevertheless, this empire was forced to bring in thousands of
troops along with heavy artillery to reinforce the repressive regime already present in the
crownland capital. All this came at a time when such reinforcements could ill be spared from
frontline service. For six days, the imperial military and gendarmes fought the nationalists in
a battle that produced three thousand casualties, the majority of whom were civilians. The
shelling and subsequent ﬁres devastated many neighborhoods of the provincial capital.
When, after a week of street ﬁghting, the imperial regime ﬁnally reestablished order in the

city, many leaders of the rebellion were shot, at least three thousand people were taken prisoner
indiscriminately, and 1,800 of them transported to be interned in camps located elsewhere in
the empire.1
Where did this ethnic nationalist revolt take place? In which empire did oppression become
so intolerable that nationalist activists in a so-called peripheral crownland actually allied
themselves with an enemy power to plan an armed uprising? In fact, the crownland capital I
have described is Dublin, and the uprising was the famed Easter Rebellion. Yet historians
have rarely considered the British Empire the site of problematic ethnic conﬂict that
substantially weakened that empire. Instead, for propagandists of the entente and to many
later historians, this kind of incident should have taken place in the Habsburg monarchy,
precisely because of the salience of the rebels’ nationalism. After all, according to so many
contemporaries—and not just to entente propagandists—Austria-Hungary was unusually
ripe for collapse compared to other European states, thanks to its alleged inability to
accommodate many warring ethnic nationalities within its frontiers, and its forceful
suppression of their legitimate demands for political autonomy. Writing from the Italian
front in 1915, for example, liberal British historian George Macaulay Trevelyan argued
typically that Austria-Hungary had long been a hotbed of nationalist discontent thanks to
the arrogant treatment the German and Hungarian masters had meted out to what he called
their Slavic “subject races.” With regard to the domestic situation of the Habsburg monarchy
directly preceding the war, Trevelyan explained: “Some people ask why, if the subject races
of Austria-Hungary were thus alienated from the Government, they did not rise in
insurrection? The answer is because all the young men were taken into the army by the
modern system of military slavery, and all the leaders were in prison or in exile.”2 By
“military slavery” Trevelyan apparently meant the system of male conscription instituted by
Austria-Hungary after the settlement of 1867, a system that some contemporaries had
actually praised for its democratizing tendencies because it applied—for the ﬁrst time—to all
social classes.3
I found this particular essay of Trevelyan’s reprinted in a series of expensively produced
volumes published in the United States after the conclusion of the war under the title The
Great Events of the Great War. Advertised as “non-partisan” and “non-sectarian,” these
volumes constituted, in the words of their editor, “an earnest effort to give the reader such
frank and full information as will enable him to comprehend clearly this greatest of all
wars.”4 And earnest they were in their effort to establish with ﬁnality the meaning of the
recently concluded war. The volumes included hundreds of translated government
documents and illustrations—mostly cartoons—from all the combatant countries. This very
comprehensiveness, the editors implied, contributed to the objectivity of their account of the
war, its origins, and its outcomes. The entire series was aimed at a broad audience made up

ﬁrstly of the men from the United States who had fought the war themselves, but directed
equally to later generations. I personally inherited a set of these volumes from my maternal
grandfather George Moulton French, a decorated veteran of the Great War. The book series
interested me especially because I have recently been curious to learn what exactly my
grandfather and his contemporaries in 1921 may have learned about the Habsburg monarchy,
its character, and its collapse in 1918. Yet while these volumes included a wealth of information
about Britain, France, Germany, and Russia, they remained relatively silent about Austria-
Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Bulgaria, Greece, Montenegro, Romania, and Serbia, to say
nothing of Albania. Even Volume I, How the Great War Arose, devoted only ﬁve of its 400 pages
to the assassination of the Archduke Francis Ferdinand (whom it mistakenly identiﬁed as the
aged Francis Joseph’s son), and a short chapter of sixteen pages dedicated to the growth of Slavic
nationalism in the Balkans and speciﬁcally to Serbia’s troubled relationship to Austria-Hungary.
That chapter, which included Trevelyan’s short explanatory essay about the monarchy, provided
its readers with a typical postwar framework for understanding the problems of the prewar
world. It was a chapter that described an anachronistic society of many national units held
together by brute force in an empire that had long outlived its raison d’être.
Ninety-nine years later, in 2014, a best-selling and respected military historian opened his
own account of the war on the Eastern Front with a sentence that could have been written
by Trevelyan in 1915: “Austria’s weakness emanated from its quarreling, disaffected
nationalities.” The same author argued that “the Habsburgs and the Ottomans were engaged
in a race to the bottom for the title of Europe’s sick man, the great power most likely to
wither and die in everyone’s lifetime.”5 The tropes of warring nationalities and of a
fundamentally moribund Austro-Hungarian state endured and even ﬂourished during the
past century, especially in literature on the First World War. But if Austria-Hungary sat
poised on the brink of extinction by nationalist revolt in 1914, why is it that the major
nationalist rebellion of World War I described above broke out in Dublin and not in
Ljubljana, L’viv, Prague, or Zagreb? Britain, although also an empire, was evidently not a
candidate for the title of sick man of Europe. No one speaks of the British state as an
anachronism in the world of the early twentieth century, despite the series of crises
precipitated by the Irish question before the war, the undemocratic power of the British
House of Lords, or the limited parliamentary franchise in Britain compared to France,
Germany, or imperial Austria. Why shouldn’t we see in the British Empire the most extreme
example of politically corrosive nationalist conﬂict within Europe, along with the ever-
growing challenges it faced to rule in its colonial empire? More importantly, why do so
many historians continue to maintain, like Trevelyan before them, that speciﬁcally
nationalist political conﬂict was the preeminent reason for the collapse of Austria-Hungary,
and that the collapse was therefore predestined long before the autumn of 1918?
A few specialist and far more non-specialist historians to this day presume (it is not even an
argument) that Austria-Hungary collapsed in 1918 largely due to popular nationalist opposition
to empire in Central Europe that had been present for decades, as if the speciﬁc experience of
four long years of war had no bearing on the question. Worse still, such normative assertions
tend to frame our understandings of the events of the 1920s following the war in Europe,
even for those of us who reject the claims of an empire existentially weakened by nationalist
conﬂict. I am not arguing that Austria-Hungary did not face political challenges centered on
issues of political nationalism, but rather that it has been made an exception to European

(New York, 2014), 15.

Editorial
Seit klassische Nationalgeschichten in der Geschichtswissenschaft eher auf dem
Rückzugsind,istdieGlobalgeschichteaufdemVormarsch.Globalgeschichtemeint
jedoch nicht einfach Geschichte »außerhalb Europas« oder »Geschichte weltweit«.
Es geht dabei um eine Geschichtsschreibung, die versucht, eurozentrische Per-
spektiven zu überwinden und das Augenmerk verstärkt auf globale Verflechtungen
und Verbindungen zu richten. Klassische Themen einer Globalgeschichte sind da-
her Kolonialismus, Migration, Handelsbeziehungen, internationale Kooperation,
Sklaverei, Tourismus, Imperialismus, Globalisierung, Wissenstransfers u.v.m.
Die Reihe Global- und Kolonialgeschichte bietet Forschungsbeiträgen zu diesen
Themen ein gemeinsames Diskussionsforum. Die Kolonialgeschichte wird dabei
als zentraler Teil der Globalgeschichte behandelt, da sie sich thematisch als Ver-
flechtungsgeschichte wie auch methodisch als Machtverhältnisse(undhegemonia-
le Diskurse) hinterfragend in diese Historiografie einordnet.

first_pages_text:
--- PAGE 1 ---
The Pillars of Dynasty: Women, Marriage Diplomacy,
and the Habsburg Dynastic Network, 1567–15701
Daniel E. Roddy
University of California, Berkeley
During the late 1560s, Philip II of Spain worked closely with an international net-
work of three female relatives—Catherine of Austria, Maria of Austria, and Juana
of Austria—to preserve and strengthen the Habsburg sphere of inﬂuence. With
their support, he managed to secure a hegemonic grip over the marriage market
and initiate different negotiations entangling Madrid, Vienna, Lisbon, and Paris.
This article analyzes their pattern of collaboration to better understand how fam-
ily members coordinated their diplomatic efforts and harmonized their response
to abrupt changes in dynastic policy. In doing so, marriage diplomacy emerges as
a protracted, volatile, and gendered process where both failure and success en-
couraged network cohesion and perpetuated Habsburg dominance over the Euro-
pean dynastic system.
DURING THE LATTER PART OF THE 1560S, the head of the House of Habsburg, King
Philip II of Spain (1527–98), exercised a hegemonic grip over the Western Euro-
pean marriage market. The scale of his machinations eclipsed anything previously
seen on the Continent, entangling the royal courts of Madrid, Vienna, Lisbon, and
Paris in complex multilateral negotiations with far-reaching implications for
Europe’s political landscape. At the center of these negotiations, both generat-
ing foreign interest in them and facilitating their progression, was an international
cohort of Habsburg women working in conjunction with Philip II, his diplomatic
agents, and one another to realize a shared dynastic vision. Comprising three rel-
atives of the Spanish king (his aunt and onetime mother-in-law, Catherine of Aus-
tria [1507–78], former queen of Portugal, and two sisters, Maria of Austria [1528–1603],
Holy Roman empress, and Juana of Austria [1535–73], princess of Portugal), this
dynastic network initially supported a plan to isolate France and reinforce kinship
ties by wedding Maria’s daughters, Anna of Austria (1549–80) and Elisabeth of
Austria (1554–92), to Philip II’s heir, Don Carlos (1545–68), and Juana’s son, King
Sebastian of Portugal (1554–78), respectively. Circumstances changed in 1568,
however, when the death of Don Carlos dramatically altered the royal marriage
pool. Thereafter, the network worked together in hopes of weaving an even greater
familial web that encompassed both Habsburg branches, the Avis and the Valois.
1Daniel Roddy is a lecturer in the History Department at the University of California, Berkeley.
He recently completed his dissertation on the evolution of Spanish Habsburg dynastic policy in the
sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
The Sixteenth Century Journal, volume 54, numbers 1–2, Spring/Summer 2023.
© 2024 Sixteenth Century Society. All rights reserved. Published by The University of Chicago Press for the Sixteenth Century Society. https://
doi.org/10.1086/727952

--- PAGE 2 ---
The present study analyzes this pattern of collaboration to show for the ﬁrst time
that the roles played by Catherine, Maria, and Juana in the construction of these
ambitious marriage projects were neither peripheral nor disconnected.2 They were
an indispensable part of Habsburg operations, underpinning the royal house’s
dominance over the European dynastic system during a critical decade.
Until now, historians have tended to unravel the complicated entanglements
of the 1560s to analyze the negotiation threads most relevant to their respective
monarchies. For instance, Alfonso Danvila’s seminal account of the unions pro-
posed for Sebastian covers diplomatic exchanges between Madrid and Lisbon,
but overlooks much of what occurred outside of the Iberian Peninsula.3 More re-
cent examples include Rubén González Cuerva’s detailed analysis of Maria’s in-
volvement in her daughters’ marriage plans, Liesbeth Geevers’s insightful study
of French dynastic policy under Catherine de’ Medici (1519–89), and Joseph F.
Patrouch’s careful examination of the negotiations from the perspective of the
Holy Roman Empire.4 Despite sustained scholarly interest in the different pro-
posals, one unintended consequence of the prevailing research has been to impose
strict geographic boundaries that did not exist in the network’s mental universe of
political action.5 Although Catherine, Maria, and Juana clearly wanted the best for
their respective kingdoms and children, they were also thinking in terms of broad
dynastic power as they ruminated over the international conﬁgurations that would
2Historians are currently working to restore the reputations of all three women. A notable exam-
ple is the exhaustive study of Maria of Austria published by Rubén González Cuerva, Maria of Austria,
Holy Roman Empress (1528–1603): Dynastic Networker (London: Routledge, 2022). The ﬁrst collection
of essays on Juana of Austria was also recently compiled by Noelia García Pérez, ed., The Making of
Juana of Austria: Gender, Art, and Patronage in Early Modern Iberia (Baton Rouge: Louisiana State
University Press, 2021). See also Annemarie Jordan Gschwend, Catarina de Áustria: A rainha
colecionadora (Lisbon: Temas e Debates, 2017); Antonio Villacorta Baños-García, La Jesuita: Juana
de Austria (Barcelona, ES: Editorial Ariel, S.A., 2005); and Annemarie Jordan Gschwend, “Catherine
of Austria: A Portuguese Queen in the Shadow of the Habsburg Court?,” Portuguese Studies Review 13
(2005): 173–94.
3Alfonso Danvila, Felipe II y El Rey Don Sebástian de Portugal (Madrid: Espasa- Calpe, S.A.,
1954), 175–94.
4Cuerva, Maria, 106–12; Liesbeth Geevers, “Ties, Triangles and Tangles: Catherine de Medici as
Philip II of Spain’s Mother-in-Law,” The Court Historian 25 (2020): 186–200; and Joseph Patrouch,
Queen’s Apprentice: Archduchess Elizabeth, Empress Maria, the Habsburgs, and the Holy Roman Em-
pire, 1554–1569 (Leiden, NL: Brill, 2010), 387–94. For further reading on the different unions, see Fer-
nando Bruquetas and Manuel Lobo, Don Carlos: Príncipe de las Españas (Madrid: Ediciones Cátedra,
2016), 193–212; Paula Sutter Fichtner, Emperor Maximilian II (New Haven, CT: Yale University Press,
2001), 105–13; Miguel Ángel Ochoa Brun, Historia de La Diplomacia Española (Madrid: Ministerios
de Asuntos Exteriores, 2000), 6:254–58; and Luis Pérez Bueno, “Del casamiento de Felipe II con su
sobrina Ana de Austria,” Hispania 7 (1947): 372–416.
5The shift from a strict state-centered approach to the study of individual actors and the socio-
cultural contexts in which they operated is the hallmark of new diplomatic history. For more on this,
see Tracey A. Sowerby, “Early Modern Diplomatic History,” History Compass 14, no. 9 (2016): 441–56;
and John Watkins, “Toward a New Diplomatic History of Medieval and Early Modern Europe,” Jour-
nal of Medieval and Early Modern Studies 38 (2008): 1–14.
4
Sixteenth Century Journal LIV/1–2 (2023)

--- PAGE 3 ---
perpetuate the glory of their natal house into the future. Daniel Nixon, Luc
Duerloo, and Liesbeth Geevers are among the scholars who have recently begun
to discuss the critical impact that this reason of dynasty, or dynastic logic, had
on Habsburg statecraft and the unfolding of international-political competition
between ruling houses.6 Critically, familial allies working together viewed the con-
stituent parts of Philip II’s grand marriage projects as being closely interconnected,
and the political fortunes of the collective participants as being tightly intertwined.
Once the scope of investigation is broadened, the extent of Catherine, Maria,
and Juana’s involvement in Habsburg marriage diplomacy becomes clear. Contrary
to scholarly depictions that have tended to underestimate their contributions, the
three women worked closely with Philip II and his ambassadors, advocated for his
proposals, and encouraged amicable relations between monarchies.7 They also ex-
ercised their maternal prerogatives to directly intercede on behalf of Habsburg in-
terests and legitimize diplomatic initiatives that originated in Spain. Tracing the
activities of this female network both complicates scholarly perceptions of the mar-
riage projects and contributes to a burgeoning historiography on the nature and
extent of women’s political participation. So far, this research has documented a
long tradition of female agency in the realms of diplomacy and international pol-
itics, underscoring the arrangement of royal unions as a crucial occasion for women
to seize, articulate, and exercise their royal authority.8 The increasing prevalence
of work on female networks has further enriched the historiography of Habs-
burg women by providing methodological and analytical tools for examining
how their activities and connections not only facilitated communication and cultural
6This mode of political thought presented a powerful and inﬂuential alternative to reason of state
thinking. Daniel H. Nexon, The Struggle for Power in Early Modern Europe: Religious Conﬂict, Dynastic
Empires, and International Change (Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 2009); Luc Duerloo,
Dynasty and Piety: Archduke Albert (1598–1621) and Habsburg Political Culture in an Age of Religious
Wars (Farnham, UK: Ashgate, 2012); and Liesbeth Geevers, “The Miracles of Spain: Dynastic Attitudes
to the Habsburg Succession and the Spanish Succession Crisis (1580–1700),” Sixteenth Century Journal
46, no. 2 (2015): 291–311.
7For example, Maria and Juana were two of Philip II’s generally ineffective female allies according
to Manuel Fernández Álvarez, Felipe II y su tiempo (Madrid: Espasa-Calpe, 1998), 799.
8Silvia Z. Mitchell, Queen, Mother, and Stateswoman: Mariana of Austria and the Government of
Spain (University Park: Pennsylvania State University Press, 2019); Helen Matheson- Pollock, Joanne
Paul, and Catherine Fletcher, eds., Queenship and Counsel in Early Modern Europe (New York: Pal-
grave Macmillan, 2018); Margaret M. McGowan, ed., Dynastic Marriages 1612/15: A Celebration of
the Habsburg and Bourbon Unions (London: Routledge, 2016); Anne J. Cruz and Mihoko Suzuki,
eds., The Rule of Women in Early Modern Europe (Champaign: University of Illinois Press, 2009);
Sharon L. Jansen, Debating Women, Politics, and Power in Early Modern Europe (New York: Palgrave
Macmillan, 2008); Laura Oliván Santaliestra, Mariana de Austria: Imagen, poder y diplomacia de una
reina cortesana (Madrid: Editorial Complutense, 2006); Katherine Crawford, Perilous Performances:
Gender and Regency in Early Modern France (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2004);
and Sharon L. Jansen, The Monstrous Regiment of Women: Female Rulers in Early Modern Europe
(New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2002).

first_pages_text:
国家制度：君主立宪
中央——地方制度：
奥地利皇帝兼匈牙利国王以及一系列头衔：帝国的统治者，可令任一忠于皇帝的党派组建帝国内阁，有权解散内阁和帝国议会可直接任免奥地利地区的神职人员
帝国议会：由皇室代表，匈牙利议会代表，其他地方民族议会代表组成。拥有立法，监督，和修改宪法和解决中央民族事务问题
皇家军事委员会∶由皇帝直接认命，负责战时军事调度指挥以及军事战略部署，主席一般是帝国最高军事统帅
匈牙利议会：由匈牙利地区民族代表组成，拥有匈牙利地区立法（除宪法外）权和有权对本地区中央管理大臣和神职人员在帝国议会提交候选名单（匈牙利地区人民拥有中央普通法法律豁免权，只遵守匈牙利议会法律）
其他地区民族议会：由其他地区民族代表组成有权对中央管理大臣和地方神职人员在帝国议会提交候选名单
帝国内阁
帝国国防部：负责奥匈帝国国防军，奥匈帝国预备役和奥匈帝国海军训练及装备革新以及和平时期征兵事宜和军官士官晋升
内政部：负责对政府经济而有效的管理
外交部：负责对外事宜以及帝国形象
财政部：负责帝国事务预算以及帝国财政收入和支出管理
内务部：负责皇室财产及日常事务管理和处理，直接向皇帝负责
行政部：负责政府日常运转和其他政府日常事务处理
帝国中央司法部：负责帝国中央法庭的日常事务和大法官的建议任命权
中央政府机构：
情报机构
1.证据局：负责为政府处理安全、防务、外事、经济方面的事物搜集情报和负责调查权力法庭
2.调查权力法庭：由证据局主导可越过现有司法机构直接审判严重危害国家安全的秘密司法机构
司法机构
1.帝国贵族法院：负责审判帝国内贵族。向皇帝负责
2.帝国中央法院：由大法官领导遵守帝国议会编纂的奥匈帝国宪法以及其由奥地利政府所编纂的奥匈帝国普通法负责审判奥地利地区
3.帝国匈牙利地方法院：由匈牙利议会领导遵守帝国议会所编纂的奥匈帝国宪法及匈牙利议会所编纂的匈牙利地区普通法负责审判匈牙利地区
4.帝国其他民族地方法院：由其他民族地区议会领导遵守帝国议会所编纂的奥匈帝国宪法及奥地利政府所编纂的奥匈帝国普通法负责审判本地民族地区
治安管理机构
帝国中央警察局：负责奥地利地区治安管理及匈牙利和其他民族地方警察局的领导和指导工作。可自行招募警员和自行采购装备
地方政府制度
匈牙利民族地方行政局：负责匈牙利地区的行政事务以及日常事务处理和其他事物处理，遵守帝国议会所编纂的奥匈帝国宪法以及匈牙利议会所编纂的匈牙利地区普通法，向匈牙利议会负责
其他民族地方行政局：负责本民族地区的行政事务以及日常事务和其他事物处理，遵守帝国议会所编纂的奥匈帝国宪法以及奥地利政府所编纂的奥匈帝国普通法，并且向地区民族议会负责
匈牙利地区议会立法局：负责收集匈牙利地区民族代表立法提议，在局内进行不透明表决后提交到匈牙利地区民族议会而后进行表决，向匈牙利地区民族议会负责，人员由匈牙利地区民族议会议会长在匈牙利地区民族议会提交候选名单经过表决后就任
匈牙利地区中央管理大臣办公处：负责监督匈牙利地区民族议会以及其他地方机构是否合法运行。直接向皇帝负责
其他民族地区中央管理大臣办公处：负责监督本地区民族议会以及其他地方机构是否合法运行。直接向皇帝负责
匈牙利民族地方行政局
匈牙利民族地方行政局内政处：匈牙利地区日常事务及其他事物管理权
